raw_evidence.label: Post-COVID expedition rebound, 22 to 279 in two years
raw_evidence.content: Annual expedition counts in the dataset show the COVID-19 collapse and recovery: only 22 expeditions in 2020 (the pandemic year), then 207 in 2021, 279 in 2022 (a 12.7x rebound from 2020), 274 in 2023, and 100 in 2024 (the 2024 figure is partial because the slice was filtered before the autumn 2024 season closed). The 2022 peak coincides with Nepal fully reopening high mountains to foreign climbers and matches the broader media narrative of a record post-pandemic boom that culminated in the 2023 Everest crowding crisis.

raw_evidence.label: 112 of 480 listed peaks remain unclimbed
raw_evidence.content: The peaks_tidy table catalogues 480 peaks: 368 marked Climbed and 112 marked Unclimbed (PSTATUS_FACTOR). Unclimbed peaks span 5,407 to 8,077 m with a median of 6,452 m - meaning that even after a century of expeditions, mountains taller than 8,000 m may still appear on the unclimbed list. The Kanti/Palchung range holds the most unclimbed peaks (14), followed by Janak/Ohmi Kangri (12), Api/Byas Risi/Guras (11), Khumbu (11) and Kangchenjunga/Simhalila (9). For climbers seeking first ascents, the western Himalaya and the Janak region remain the frontier.

raw_evidence.label: Spring 2023 was the deadliest Everest season ever
raw_evidence.content: The 2020-2024 window in this dataset coincides with a structural transformation of Himalayan climbing. The 2020 season was effectively cancelled by COVID-19. Then Nepal threw the gates wide open: in spring 2023 the government issued a record 478 Everest permits, and at least 17 climbers died, making it the deadliest Everest season in history. With an average support team of 1.5 Sherpas per client, more than 1,200 people queued for the high camps that one spring. Kami Rita Sherpa pushed his personal Everest record to 28 ascents the same year. In 2024 Nepal's Supreme Court ordered limits on Everest permits, citing overcrowding. So the 2020-2024 slice captures both the pandemic shutdown and the post-pandemic boom that triggered regulatory backlash.

raw_evidence.label: Why supplemental oxygen matters above 8,000 m
raw_evidence.content: Above roughly 7,500 m climbers enter the so-called 'death zone' where atmospheric oxygen is about a third of sea-level values and the human body cannot acclimatize indefinitely. Bottled oxygen lowers the effective altitude experienced by the body, dramatically improving cognition, endurance and survival odds. The exped_tidy table tracks this with a granular set of logical columns: O2USED (any bottled oxygen on the climb), O2NONE (an explicit 'no oxygen' attempt), O2CLIMB (climbing with O2), O2DESCENT (descending with O2), O2SLEEP (sleeping with O2), O2MEDICAL (used medically only), O2TAKEN (carried but not used), and O2UNKWN. Commercial Manaslu expeditions today supply roughly two bottles per member and one per Sherpa, and roughly half of clients elect to use it. Everest's mortality drop is largely attributed to obligatory oxygen for guides plus standardised rope-fixing.

raw_evidence.label: Oxygen lifts success rate by 38 percentage points
raw_evidence.content: Of 882 expeditions, 409 used bottled oxygen and 473 did not. Oxygen-using expeditions succeeded 94.4% of the time (386/409) versus 56.7% (268/473) for no-oxygen expeditions - a 37.7 percentage-point gap. Bottled oxygen, in this slice, is the single strongest predictor of summit success of any binary variable in the dataset. The mechanism is straightforward (det_06): above 7,500 m the body cannot acclimatize indefinitely and oxygen lowers the effective altitude, restoring cognition and stamina. This figure echoes the Everest mortality drop attributed to obligatory oxygen for guides.
raw_evidence.code:
o2_used = exped[exped["O2USED"] == True]
o2_not  = exped[exped["O2USED"] == False]
print(f"\nO2 used: n={len(o2_used)} success={o2_used['IS_SUCCESS'].mean()*100:.1f}%")
print(f"O2 not used: n={len(o2_not)} success={o2_not['IS_SUCCESS'].mean()*100:.1f}%")

# --- ana_07: Death rate by oxygen use ---
print("\n=== ana_07 ===")
o2_deaths = exped.groupby("O2USED")["TOTAL_DEATHS"].agg(["size", "sum", "mean"])
print(o2_deaths.to_string())

raw_evidence.label: Among failures, weather is king (34%); technical difficulty is marginal (4%)
raw_evidence.content: Restricting to the 228 expeditions that did NOT succeed, the failure mix shifts dramatically: bad weather alone explains 34.2% of failures (78/228), and bad conditions another 23.7% (54/228). Together, weather and conditions account for 57.9% of expedition failures. Pure technical difficulty - the romantic image of climbers turned back by an unclimbable cliff - explains just 3.95% of failures (9/228). Illness/AMS/frostbite explains 11.0% (25/228), and outright accidents 2.2% (5/228). The picture is dominated by environmental hindrances rather than individual climbing limits, an important framing for the modern, commercially-supported era.

raw_evidence.label: Sherpas are 32% of recorded deaths but earn the same death rate per person
raw_evidence.content: Across 2020-2024, the dataset records 36 member deaths and 17 hired-staff (Sherpa and other) deaths, for 53 total. Hired staff make up 32.1% of all recorded deaths despite being roughly 48% of the people on the mountain (6,716 hired vs 7,226 members). Per-person death rates: members 4.98 per 1,000, hired 2.53 per 1,000. The gap reflects two things: clients without Sherpa-level acclimatisation are statistically more vulnerable, and Sherpas often turn back with clients before fatal exposure. The figure also disguises the fact that almost all hired deaths cluster around Everest where the icefall and crowding hit Sherpas disproportionately.

total_m = int(exped["MDEATHS"].sum())
total_h = int(exped["HDEATHS"].sum())
total_mem = int(exped["TOTMEMBERS"].sum())
total_hired = int(exped["TOTHIRED"].sum())
print(f"Member deaths: {total_m}")
print(f"Hired (Sherpa) deaths: {total_h}")
print(f"Total deaths: {total_m+total_h}")
print(f"Hired share of deaths: {total_h/(total_m+total_h)*100:.1f}%")
print(f"Member-death rate per person: {total_m/total_mem*1000:.2f} per 1000")
print(f"Hired-death rate per person: {total_h/total_hired*1000:.2f} per 1000")
print(f"Total members: {total_mem}, total hired: {total_hired}")

raw_evidence.label: Termination reason mix: 71% success, 9% bad weather
raw_evidence.content: Combining all three success codes (main peak, subpeak, claimed), 74.1% of all 2020-2024 expeditions ended successfully (628 main peak + 26 subpeak = 654 of 882). raw_evidence.label: Sherpas are 32% of recorded deaths but earn the same death rate per person
raw_evidence.content: Across 2020-2024, the dataset records 36 member deaths and 17 hired-staff (Sherpa and other) deaths, for 53 total. Hired staff make up 32.1% of all recorded deaths despite being roughly 48% of the people on the mountain (6,716 hired vs 7,226 members). Per-person death rates: members 4.98 per 1,000, hired 2.53 per 1,000. The gap reflects two things: clients without Sherpa-level acclimatisation are statistically more vulnerable, and Sherpas often turn back with clients before fatal exposure. The figure also disguises the fact that almost all hired deaths cluster around Everest where the icefall and crowding hit Sherpas disproportionately.

raw_evidence.label: Spring 2023 was the deadliest Everest season ever
raw_evidence.content: The 2020-2024 window in this dataset coincides with a structural transformation of Himalayan climbing. The 2020 season was effectively cancelled by COVID-19. Then Nepal threw the gates wide open: in spring 2023 the government issued a record 478 Everest permits, and at least 17 climbers died, making it the deadliest Everest season in history. With an average support team of 1.5 Sherpas per client, more than 1,200 people queued for the high camps that one spring. Kami Rita Sherpa pushed his personal Everest record to 28 ascents the same year. In 2024 Nepal's Supreme Court ordered limits on Everest permits, citing overcrowding. So the 2020-2024 slice captures both the pandemic shutdown and the post-pandemic boom that triggered regulatory backlash.

raw_evidence.label: What the Nepal Himalaya actually is
raw_evidence.content: The peaks_tidy table classifies each peak by HIMAL_FACTOR (mountain range) and REGION_FACTOR (broader region). The Nepal Himalaya is conventionally split into seven regions running west to east: Kangchenjunga-Janak, Khumbu-Rolwaling-Makalu, Langtang-Jugal, Manaslu-Ganesh, Annapurna-Damodar-Peri, Dhaulagiri-Mukut, and Kanjiroba-Far West. Within these sit the famous sub-ranges - Khumbu (which holds Everest, Lhotse, Cho Oyu), Annapurna, Manaslu/Mansiri, Dhaulagiri, Kangchenjunga, Makalu, plus many smaller groups. Eight of the world's fourteen 'eight-thousanders' (peaks above 8,000 m) lie wholly or partly in Nepal: Everest, Kangchenjunga, Lhotse, Makalu, Cho Oyu, Dhaulagiri, Manaslu and Annapurna. Heights in peaks_tidy are stored both in metres (HEIGHTM) and feet (HEIGHTF). Status is encoded in PSTATUS_FACTOR with values 'Climbed', 'Unclimbed', and 'Unknown'.

raw_evidence.label: Three peaks absorb half of all expeditions
raw_evidence.content: Of the 480 catalogued peaks in the Nepal Himalaya, just three accounted for 49.0% of all 2020-2024 expeditions: Everest (189, 21.4%), Ama Dablam (147, 16.7%) and Manaslu (96, 10.9%). The next tier - Lhotse (79), Himlung Himal (51), Dhaulagiri I (35), Makalu (26), Baruntse (24), Annapurna I (22), Kangchenjunga (20) - confirms that climbing tourism is dominated by a small set of marquee peaks. Ama Dablam at 6,812 m is famous for being a 'high altitude trophy' with technical climbing but a lower oxygen-debt; Everest, Manaslu and Lhotse are 8000ers commercialised with fixed-rope highways.
raw_evidence.code:

g["rate"] = g["success"] / g["n"] * 100
g = g[g["n"] >= 10].sort_values("rate", ascending=False)

raw_evidence.label: Annapurna I is the deadliest 8000er; Everest is no longer 14% lethal
raw_evidence.content: Per the Himalayan Database itself, Annapurna I has the highest cumulative fatality-to-summit ratio of the fourteen 8000ers - 13.42% as of February 2025 (75 deaths against 559 ascents), with most deaths concentrated at a single avalanche zone around 5,900 m between Camps II and III. By contrast Everest's mortality rate, which was about 14.5% from 1922-1999, has fallen to roughly 1-3% in the 2000-2023 era thanks to obligatory oxygen, fixed-rope infrastructure, weather forecasting and helicopter rescue. The Himalayan Database is the canonical source quoted across these statistics. Within the 2020-2024 slice we should expect Annapurna and Dhaulagiri to look disproportionately dangerous, while Everest looks crowded but survivable.

raw_evidence.label: TERMREASON, the heart of the expedition story
raw_evidence.content: Each row in exped_tidy ends with a TERMREASON code (1-14). Codes 1-3 mean success ('Success (main peak)', 'Success (subpeak, foresummit)', 'Success (claimed)'). Codes 4-12 enumerate failure modes: 4 'Bad weather (storms, high winds)', 5 'Bad conditions (deep snow, avalanching, falling ice or rock)', 6 'Accident (death or serious injury)', 7 'Illness, AMS, exhaustion or frostbite', 8 'Lack (or loss) of supplies, support or equipment', 9 'Lack of time', 10 'Route technically too difficult, lack of experience, strength or motivation', 11 'Did not reach base camp', 12 'Did not attempt climb'. Code 13 is 'Attempt rumored' and 14 is 'Other'. This is the single richest categorical column in the dataset because it answers the dramatic question every expedition narrative ends with: did they get up, and if not, what stopped them?

Pure technical failure - 'Route technically too difficult, lack of experience, strength or motivation' - is rare at 9 expeditions (1.02%), and accident-driven termination is rarer still at 5 expeditions (0.57%).

raw_evidence.label: Among failures, weather is king (34%); technical difficulty is marginal (4%)
raw_evidence.content: Restricting to the 228 expeditions that did NOT succeed, the failure mix shifts dramatically: bad weather alone explains 34.2% of failures (78/228), and bad conditions another 23.7% (54/228). Together, weather and conditions account for 57.9% of expedition failures. Pure technical difficulty - the romantic image of climbers turned back by an unclimbable cliff - explains just 3.95% of failures (9/228). Illness/AMS/frostbite explains 11.0% (25/228), and outright accidents 2.2% (5/228). The picture is dominated by environmental hindrances rather than individual climbing limits, an important framing for the modern, commercially-supported era.

sentences.summary: det_06: Why supplemental oxygen matters above 8,000 m. Source: Eight-thousander - Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight-thousander) Facts: Above 7,500 m the air pressure is about a third of sea level and the body cannot acclimatize indefinitely; Safety improvements on 8000ers are attributed to obligatory oxygen for guides, better infrastructure and weather forecasts

raw_evidence.label: Why supplemental oxygen matters above 8,000 m
raw_evidence.content: Above roughly 7,500 m climbers enter the so-called 'death zone' where atmospheric oxygen is about a third of sea-level values and the human body cannot acclimatize indefinitely. Bottled oxygen lowers the effective altitude experienced by the body, dramatically improving cognition, endurance and survival odds. The exped_tidy table tracks this with a granular set of logical columns: O2USED (any bottled oxygen on the climb), O2NONE (an explicit 'no oxygen' attempt), O2CLIMB (climbing with O2), O2DESCENT (descending with O2), O2SLEEP (sleeping with O2), O2MEDICAL (used medically only), O2TAKEN (carried but not used), and O2UNKWN. Commercial Manaslu expeditions today supply roughly two bottles per member and one per Sherpa, and roughly half of clients elect to use it. Everest's mortality drop is largely attributed to obligatory oxygen for guides plus standardised rope-fixing.

raw_evidence.label: What the Nepal Himalaya actually is
raw_evidence.content: The peaks_tidy table classifies each peak by HIMAL_FACTOR (mountain range) and REGION_FACTOR (broader region). The Nepal Himalaya is conventionally split into seven regions running west to east: Kangchenjunga-Janak, Khumbu-Rolwaling-Makalu, Langtang-Jugal, Manaslu-Ganesh, Annapurna-Damodar-Peri, Dhaulagiri-Mukut, and Kanjiroba-Far West. Within these sit the famous sub-ranges - Khumbu (which holds Everest, Lhotse, Cho Oyu), Annapurna, Manaslu/Mansiri, Dhaulagiri, Kangchenjunga, Makalu, plus many smaller groups. Eight of the world's fourteen 'eight-thousanders' (peaks above 8,000 m) lie wholly or partly in Nepal: Everest, Kangchenjunga, Lhotse, Makalu, Cho Oyu, Dhaulagiri, Manaslu and Annapurna. Heights in peaks_tidy are stored both in metres (HEIGHTM) and feet (HEIGHTF). Status is encoded in PSTATUS_FACTOR with values 'Climbed', 'Unclimbed', and 'Unknown'.

raw_evidence.label: Annapurna I is the deadliest 8000er; Everest is no longer 14% lethal
raw_evidence.content: Per the Himalayan Database itself, Annapurna I has the highest cumulative fatality-to-summit ratio of the fourteen 8000ers - 13.42% as of February 2025 (75 deaths against 559 ascents), with most deaths concentrated at a single avalanche zone around 5,900 m between Camps II and III. By contrast Everest's mortality rate, which was about 14.5% from 1922-1999, has fallen to roughly 1-3% in the 2000-2023 era thanks to obligatory oxygen, fixed-rope infrastructure, weather forecasting and helicopter rescue. The Himalayan Database is the canonical source quoted across these statistics. Within the 2020-2024 slice we should expect Annapurna and Dhaulagiri to look disproportionately dangerous, while Everest looks crowded but survivable.

raw_evidence.label: Annapurna I is the deadliest 8000er; Everest is no longer 14% lethal
raw_evidence.content: Per the Himalayan Database itself, Annapurna I has the highest cumulative fatality-to-summit ratio of the fourteen 8000ers - 13.42% as of February 2025 (75 deaths against 559 ascents), with most deaths concentrated at a single avalanche zone around 5,900 m between Camps II and III. The Himalayan Database is the canonical source quoted across these statistics. Within the 2020-2024 slice we should expect Annapurna and Dhaulagiri to look disproportionately dangerous, while Everest looks crowded but survivable.

raw_evidence.label: Eight-thousanders: 55% of all expeditions, wildly different death rates
raw_evidence.content: The eight 8000ers in the Nepal Himalaya absorbed 483 of 882 expeditions (54.8%) in 2020-2024. The death rate per 1,000 people-on-mountain ranges from 0.0 (Cho Oyu, n=212 climbers, 0 deaths) up to 7.30 on Everest (4,659 climbers, 34 deaths) and 6.08 on Kangchenjunga (329 climbers, 2 deaths). Success rates also span widely: from 89.4% on Everest and 86.4% on Annapurna I (n=22 expeditions only, much smaller than the cumulative 13.4% Annapurna fatality rate quoted by Guinness in det_04) down to 51.4% on Dhaulagiri I and 62.5% on Cho Oyu. This slice is too small to overturn the long-run reputation of any peak; it's a snapshot of recent traffic, not history.
raw_evidence.code:
sub = exped[exped["PEAK_NAME"].isin(EIGHT_K)].copy()
print(f"Eight-thousander expeditions in slice: {len(sub)} ({len(sub)/len(exped)*100:.1f}% of all)")
g8 = sub.groupby("PEAK_NAME").agg(
    n=("IS_SUCCESS", "size"),
    success=("IS_SUCCESS", "sum"),
    member_deaths=("MDEATHS", "sum"),
    hired_deaths=("HDEATHS", "sum"),
    total_members=("TOTMEMBERS", "sum"),
    total_hired=("TOTHIRED", "sum"),
)
g8["success_rate"] = (g8["success"] / g8["n"] * 100).round(2)
g8["death_rate_per1000"] = ((g8["member_deaths"] + g8["hired_deaths"]) / (g8["total_members"] + g8["total_hired"]) * 1000).round(2)
g8["height_m"] = g8.index.map(lambda p: peaks.set_index("PKNAME").loc[p, "HEIGHTM"] if p in peaks["PKNAME"].values else None)
g8 = g8.sort_values("height_m", ascending=False)
print(g8.to_string())

Source: Eight-thousander - Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight-thousander) Facts: Above 7,500 m the air pressure is about a third of sea level and the body cannot acclimatize indefinitely; Safety improvements on 8000ers are attributed to obligatory oxygen for guides, better infrastructure and weather forecasts

raw_evidence.label: Why supplemental oxygen matters above 8,000 m
raw_evidence.content: Above roughly 7,500 m climbers enter the so-called 'death zone' where atmospheric oxygen is about a third of sea-level values and the human body cannot acclimatize indefinitely. Bottled oxygen lowers the effective altitude experienced by the body, dramatically improving cognition, endurance and survival odds. The exped_tidy table tracks this with a granular set of logical columns: O2USED (any bottled oxygen on the climb), O2NONE (an explicit 'no oxygen' attempt), O2CLIMB (climbing with O2), O2DESCENT (descending with O2), O2SLEEP (sleeping with O2), O2MEDICAL (used medically only), O2TAKEN (carried but not used), and O2UNKWN. Commercial Manaslu expeditions today supply roughly two bottles per member and one per Sherpa, and roughly half of clients elect to use it. Everest's mortality drop is largely attributed to obligatory oxygen for guides plus standardised rope-fixing.

raw_evidence.label: Sherpas are 32% of recorded deaths but earn the same death rate per person
raw_evidence.content: Across 2020-2024, the dataset records 36 member deaths and 17 hired-staff (Sherpa and other) deaths, for 53 total. Hired staff make up 32.1% of all recorded deaths despite being roughly 48% of the people on the mountain (6,716 hired vs 7,226 members). Per-person death rates: members 4.98 per 1,000, hired 2.53 per 1,000. The gap reflects two things: clients without Sherpa-level acclimatisation are statistically more vulnerable, and Sherpas often turn back with clients before fatal exposure. The figure also disguises the fact that almost all hired deaths cluster around Everest where the icefall and crowding hit Sherpas disproportionately.

total_h = int(exped["HDEATHS"].sum())
total_mem = int(exped["TOTMEMBERS"].sum())
total_hired = int(exped["TOTHIRED"].sum())
print(f"Member deaths: {total_m}")
print(f"Hired (Sherpa) deaths: {total_h}")
print(f"Total deaths: {total_m+total_h}")
print(f"Hired share of deaths: {total_h/(total_m+total_h)*100:.1f}%")
print(f"Member-death rate per person: {total_m/total_mem*1000:.2f} per 1000")
print(f"Hired-death rate per person: {total_h/total_hired*1000:.2f} per 1000")
print(f"Total members: {total_mem}, total hired: {total_hired}")

raw_evidence.label: No-hired expeditions: 30 points lower success, far smaller scale
raw_evidence.content: Expeditions with NO hired personnel above base camp (the alpine-style purist mode) had a 48.6% success rate (n=146), compared with 79.2% for expeditions that employed hired staff (n=736). Member deaths in no-hired teams: 5 of 519 climbers; in hired teams: 31 of 6,707. Per-climber member death rates therefore look comparable, but the no-hired teams achieved their successes with one-tenth the support, and on a different mix of peaks.

raw_evidence.label: TERMREASON, the heart of the expedition story
raw_evidence.content: Each row in exped_tidy ends with a TERMREASON code (1-14). Codes 1-3 mean success ('Success (main peak)', 'Success (subpeak, foresummit)', 'Success (claimed)'). Codes 4-12 enumerate failure modes: 4 'Bad weather (storms, high winds)', 5 'Bad conditions (deep snow, avalanching, falling ice or rock)', 6 'Accident (death or serious injury)', 7 'Illness, AMS, exhaustion or frostbite', 8 'Lack (or loss) of supplies, support or equipment', 9 'Lack of time', 10 'Route technically too difficult, lack of experience, strength or motivation', 11 'Did not reach base camp', 12 'Did not attempt climb'. Code 13 is 'Attempt rumored' and 14 is 'Other'. This is the single richest categorical column in the dataset because it answers the dramatic question every expedition narrative ends with: did they get up, and if not, what stopped them?

raw_evidence.label: Spring (52%) and Autumn (45%) own the calendar; Winter is brutal
raw_evidence.content: Seasonality is bimodal. Spring (Mar-May) hosts 52.4% of expeditions (462), Autumn (Sep-Nov) 44.7% (394), Summer just 0.6% (5) and Winter 2.4% (21). Success rates are 77.1% in Spring, 72.8% in Autumn, 60.0% in Summer (n only 5), and a stark 38.1% in Winter. Spring's combination of pre-monsoon stable weather, established rope-fixing, and the famous May summit window keeps it on top; Winter's collapse to 38% reflects unforgiving Himalayan winter weather even when expeditions still attempt it.
raw_evidence.code:
season_total = exped["SEASON_FACTOR"].value_counts()
season_pct = (season_total / season_total.sum() * 100).round(2)
season_success = exped.groupby("SEASON_FACTOR")["IS_SUCCESS"].agg(["size", "mean"])
season_success["pct"] = (season_success["mean"] * 100).round(2)
print("Counts:", season_total.to_dict())
print("Pct:", season_pct.to_dict())
print("\nSuccess by season:")
print(season_success.to_string())

raw_evidence.label: Why this dataset matters
raw_evidence.content: Himalayan mountaineering is one of the few extreme adventure pursuits with a near-complete public record, and that record drives concrete policy. The Himalayan Database underpins fatality statistics quoted in journalism, the rule changes Nepal's government implements, and the marketing of commercial expeditions. The 2020-2024 slice analysed here captures the moment commercialised high-altitude climbing entered its largest scale ever - and started running into crowding, regulation and rising body counts. For a general reader the data offers a rare quantitative window into a culture (Sherpa labour, summit fever, oxygen ethics) that is mostly experienced through hagiographic memoirs rather than numbers.

raw_evidence.label: What the Nepal Himalaya actually is
raw_evidence.content: The peaks_tidy table classifies each peak by HIMAL_FACTOR (mountain range) and REGION_FACTOR (broader region). The Nepal Himalaya is conventionally split into seven regions running west to east: Kangchenjunga-Janak, Khumbu-Rolwaling-Makalu, Langtang-Jugal, Manaslu-Ganesh, Annapurna-Damodar-Peri, Dhaulagiri-Mukut, and Kanjiroba-Far West. Within these sit the famous sub-ranges - Khumbu (which holds Everest, Lhotse, Cho Oyu), Annapurna, Manaslu/Mansiri, Dhaulagiri, Kangchenjunga, Makalu, plus many smaller groups. Eight of the world's fourteen 'eight-thousanders' (peaks above 8,000 m) lie wholly or partly in Nepal: Everest, Kangchenjunga, Lhotse, Makalu, Cho Oyu, Dhaulagiri, Manaslu and Annapurna. Heights in peaks_tidy are stored both in metres (HEIGHTM) and feet (HEIGHTF). Status is encoded in PSTATUS_FACTOR with values 'Climbed', 'Unclimbed', and 'Unknown'.

raw_evidence.label: Origin: Elizabeth Hawley and the Himalayan Database
raw_evidence.content: The Himalayan Database is a comprehensive archive of mountaineering expeditions in the Nepal Himalaya. It was built around the lifetime work of Elizabeth Hawley (1923-2018), an American journalist who moved from a research role at Fortune magazine in New York to Kathmandu in 1959 and became a Reuters correspondent in 1962. From her Kathmandu apartment she interviewed nearly every expedition entering or leaving Nepal, cross-checking summit claims with such tenacity that the climbing community nicknamed her 'the Sherlock Holmes of the mountaineering world'. In 1992 she partnered with Canadian programmer Richard Salisbury to digitize her notes. The first published edition appeared in 2004 as a CD-ROM booklet from the American Alpine Club. After Hawley's death in 2018, the non-profit organization 'The Himalayan Database' continues to maintain and freely distribute the archive (Version 2). The TidyTuesday slice released on 2025-01-21 contains two tidy tables (peaks_tidy with 480 peaks and exped_tidy filtered to expeditions with year 2020-2024) so this blog focuses on the modern, post-pandemic era of Himalayan climbing.
